This is the end-to-end workflow behind [the pitch](day16_pump_screen_offers.html)
— from the raw PDI tables to a single offer on the pump screen. **Scroll inside
the diagram** to move through the pipeline, and **click any box** — the detail
appears underneath.

**This page answers *why*** — why the label looks like that, why two models,
why the decision is priced the way it is. For ***what to build*** — table
schemas, grains and the PySpark that feeds each one to the model — see
[**pipeline v2 →**](pipeline2.html). Every column in the source data is
described in the [**data dictionary →**](data-dict.html).

The diagram is generated, not drawn: [`img/pump_pipeline.py`](img/pump_pipeline.py)
renders it with Graphviz, so it cannot drift from the design. There is also a
[flat PNG](img/pump_pipeline.png) for slides and printing.

::: {#d-start .node-detail}
### Pick a box

Every step below is something a team has to actually build. The boxes in
**orange** are the ones we constructed rather than read — the unit of
analysis and its label. Those are where the real decisions live.

| Colour | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Orange | We constructed it |
| Red | A trap, or something we don't have |
| Teal | A trained model |
| Green | The decision, in dollars |

The scripts behind every figure live in `data/` in the course repo:
`explore.py`, `pump_visit_labels.py`, `daypart_signal.py`,
`uplift_feasibility.py`, `promo_event_study.py` and `data-dict.yaml`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Where the figures come from.** One run over the PDI extract — 940 stores in
eight Intermountain West states, October 2024 to September 2026. The models
themselves are fitted on a 24-store pilot subset; exploration figures are
full-estate, and the two are not mixed.
:::
:::

::: {#d-items .node-detail}
### transaction-items-all

**128,599,042 rows**, one per item rung up, across 71.7M transactions and 940
stores.

```python
pl.scan_parquet("transaction-items-all/*.parquet").select(
    "TRANSACTION_SET_ID",  # the basket key
    "STORE_ID", "DATE_TIME",
    "GTIN",                # barcode, or a placeholder when keyed
    "UNIT_QUANTITY", "GRAND_TOTAL_AMOUNT",
    "SCAN_TYPE",           # GTIN | NONSCAN | PLU | FMT_ERR
    "NONSCAN_CATEGORY",    # NACS dept for keyed lines — FUEL lives here
    "NONSCAN_SUBCATEGORY", # fuel grade lives here
)
```

58.9% of lines are scanned barcodes; the rest are keyed departments. **Fuel is
28% of lines and $1.55B of $2.08B revenue.**
:::

::: {#d-shopper .node-detail}
### shopper-id

**71,790,254 rows**, one per payment. Every transaction in this extract has a
shopper — the unidentified ones were dropped before delivery.

```python
shopper = (pl.scan_parquet("shopper-id/*.parquet")
    .select("TRANSACTION_SET_ID", "SHOPPER_ID")
    .unique(subset="TRANSACTION_SET_ID"))  # split tender → duplicate rows
```

`SHOPPER_ID` is `hash(card BIN + last 4 + store state)`. Two consequences worth
stating to a client:

- The same card in **two states is two shoppers**, so cross-border travel is invisible.
- BIN + last 4 is not unique to a card, so a few ids are more than one person.

8.0M shoppers, median **2 transactions** each.
:::

::: {#d-gtin .node-detail}
### master-gtin

**99,074 products**, one row per barcode, 35 PDI categories.

```python
gtin = (pl.scan_parquet("master-gtin/*.parquet")
    .select("GTIN", "CATEGORY", "SUBCATEGORY", "BRAND")
    .unique(subset="GTIN"))
```

Matches **88% of scanned lines**. Two cautions:

- `CATEGORY` is PDI's taxonomy; `NONSCAN_CATEGORY` is NACS. Coalescing them
  mixes vocabularies.
- Every row was last updated **2024-07-03**, before our transaction window
  opens. Products launched since will never match.
:::

::: {#d-stores .node-detail}
### stores-information

36,912 stores in the master, but only **940 appear in our transactions** — all
of them resolvable, in eight Intermountain West states.

| State | Stores |
|---|---|
| CO | 221 |
| UT | 164 |
| AZ | 158 |
| ID | 111 |
| NV, NM, MT, WY | 286 |

The column that matters most is `START_WEEK_CONTINUOUS_DATA` — the first week a
store reports without gaps. **Filter on it before any time series**, or stores
joining the panel will look like growth.
:::

::: {#d-clean .node-detail}
### Clean lines

Two filters and a coalesce. This is the whole of it:

```python
lines = (items
    .filter((pl.col("UNIT_QUANTITY").cast(pl.Float64) > 0)
            & (pl.col("GRAND_TOTAL_AMOUNT").cast(pl.Float64) > 0))
    .join(gtin, on="GTIN", how="left")
    .with_columns(category=pl.coalesce("CATEGORY", "NONSCAN_CATEGORY"))
    .drop_nulls("category"))
```

The filters remove **481,568 voids** and **701,406 returns**. The coalesce
labels **85.6% of lines**; the rest are scanned items missing from the master.

Every money column is `Decimal(38, x)`. Cast to `Float64` on read or the
arithmetic is slow and occasionally surprising.
:::

::: {#d-drop .node-detail}
### Drop non-purchases

The rule is **not** "drop SERVICES". It is **drop anything the customer didn't
choose.**

```python
NOT_A_PURCHASE = ["FUEL", "SERVICES"]   # fuel is the anchor, not the outcome
```

`SERVICES` is **99.5% card-processing fees** of about $0.35, charged on the fuel
sale itself:

| NONSCAN_DETAIL | Lines | Avg |
|---|---|---|
| CREDIT CARD FEE | 3,940,565 | $0.35 |
| LABOR | 5,030 | $68.69 |
| POST OFFICE | 666 | $21.05 |

Counting the fee as an in-store purchase leaks the fuel transaction into its own
label. **It inflated the attach rate by about seven points.** A model trained on
it learns *"customers who pay by card buy SERVICES"* — perfectly accurate,
perfectly useless.
:::

::: {#d-visit .node-detail}
### Fuel visit {.orange-head}

The unit of analysis, and the decision a team has to defend. A visit is every
purchase by the same shopper from **15 minutes before** the fuel transaction to
**45 minutes after**.

```python
BEFORE, AFTER = 15, 45

# Hour buckets keep the join small; the window spans at most three of them,
# so each candidate is offered to its bucket and both neighbours.
shifted = pl.concat([
    store.with_columns(bucket=pl.col("bucket") + pl.duration(hours=k))
    for k in (-1, 0, 1)])

delta = (pl.col("ts_store") - pl.col("ts")).dt.total_minutes()
hit = fuel.join(shifted, on=["SHOPPER_ID", "bucket"], how="left").filter(
    (delta >= -BEFORE) & (delta <= AFTER))
```

Asymmetric because most people fuel first. The timing says it's generous, not
tight:

| Relative to the pump | Share |
|---|---|
| −15 to 0 *(shopped first)* | 16.2% |
| **0 to 5 min** | **77.2%** |
| 5 to 15 min | 5.3% |
| 15 to 45 min | 1.3% |

Only 48,113 of 4.6M converting visits involve a second store, so dropping the
same-store constraint costs nothing.
:::

::: {#d-label .node-detail}
### The label {.orange-head}

**36,142,617 fuel visits. 12.8% buy something inside.** Median in-store spend
when they do: **$7.87**.

```python
basket = fuel.join(
    hit.group_by("fuel_tx").agg(n_store_tx=pl.col("store_tx").n_unique()),
    on="fuel_tx", how="left",
).with_columns(bought=pl.col("n_store_tx").fill_null(0) > 0)
```

This column does not exist in the data. **We built it**, and every number
downstream inherits whatever we got wrong here. That is why the window and the
`SERVICES` filter are worth a slide each.

About 1 in 8 — the base rate every model has to beat.
:::

::: {#d-ctx .node-detail}
### Context features

Everything knowable **before the nozzle goes back**. The card is read before the
fuel flows, so identity is available too.

```python
ctx = basket.with_columns(
    hour=pl.col("ts").dt.hour(),        # store wall-clock, per PDI
    weekday=pl.col("ts").dt.weekday(),
    month=pl.col("ts").dt.month(),
    # grade comes from NONSCAN_SUBCATEGORY: REGULAR, DIESEL, MID/PLUS, ...
)
```

`DATE_TIME` is documented as **the wall clock time for the store**, so dayparts
need no timezone conversion — worth confirming, because the panel spans four
time zones.

Signal strength, measured:

| Feature | Spread in attach |
|---|---|
| Hour | 7.5% (2am) → **15.1%** (6am) |
| Fuel grade | 12.2% → 13.3% — *almost nothing* |

A variable being available doesn't make it useful.
:::

::: {#d-hist .node-detail}
### History features

Per category, computed **strictly from visits before the one being scored**.
This is the leakage rule with a clock on it.

```python
from pyspark.sql import Window
w = (Window.partitionBy("SHOPPER_ID", "category")
          .orderBy("ts").rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, -1))

df = (df
  .withColumn("bought_before", F.max("bought").over(w))
  .withColumn("prior_share",   F.avg("bought").over(w))
  .withColumn("days_since",    F.datediff("ts", F.max("ts").over(w))))
```

`rowsBetween(..., -1)` is the whole trick — it excludes the current row.

**History barely predicts whether they come inside** (12.6% with none, 12.5%
with 10+), but it is the best signal for *what* they buy. That asymmetry is why
there are two models instead of one.
:::

::: {#d-relevance .node-detail}
### Category Relevance {.teal-head}

**Will they buy category X on this fill?** Classification — six calibrated
binary classifiers (`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`), one per category, each
scoring every visit.

```python
for cat in TOP6:                       # six independent binaries
    y = F.array_contains("cats", cat).cast("int")
    models[cat] = GBTClassifier(labelCol="y").fit(train.withColumn("y", y))
```

**Not a multiclass model.** A basket holds several categories at once, so a
softmax would force them to compete and return numbers we cannot price.

**Not rebalanced.** The output is multiplied by dollars; a model trained on a
balanced sample scores an average visit at 0.5 instead of its base rate and
inflates every expected value about 4×.

The strongest single feature is the shopper's own **prior attach rate**. How
*many* times we have seen someone is worth +0.004 AUC; what *share* of those
visits ended inside is worth +0.109.

| Category | Out-of-time AUC |
|---|---|
| Cigarettes | 0.899 |
| Beer | 0.892 |
| Other Tobacco | 0.880 |
| Packaged Beverages | 0.814 |
| Candy | 0.786 |
| Salty Snacks | 0.783 |
:::

::: {#d-affinity .node-detail}
### SKU Affinity {.teal-head}

**Which item inside the category?** Alternating least squares on implicit
feedback — Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008).

```python
als = ALS(userCol="shopper_ix", itemCol="item_ix", ratingCol="n",
          implicitPrefs=True,        # counts are confidence, not ratings
          rank=32, regParam=0.05, alpha=20, coldStartStrategy="drop")
```

**The item key is `gtin@daypart`.** ALS takes no features, so the only way to
give it a clock is to put one in the key — and the clock matters: same-daypart
purchase pairs repeat the same SKU 18.0% of the time against 10.0% across
dayparts.

**SKU, not brand.** At brand level ALS scores **0.88× popularity** — worse
than showing the best seller. With a handful of brands that matter there is
nothing personal left to learn; the long tail of SKUs is what gives the model
something to do.

Measured on the held-out period, over the fills where ALS actually ran and
the customer bought inside the offered category:

| | hit@1 | hit@10 |
|---|---|---|
| ALS, SKU level | **9.1%** | 34.3% |
| Store best seller | 3.2% | 16.9% |
| | **2.8×** | 2.0× |

**hit@1 is the operational number** — the screen shows one offer. Over all
fills, personalised and fallback together, it is 6.2% against 2.9%.

Scores are normalised **within a category**, so the number means *given they
buy this category, which item* — which is what the decision multiplies
against `P(category)`.

**This model only ever ranks inside one category.** Category Relevance picks
the category first, on probability alone, and SKU Affinity is confined to it.
Ranking the whole catalog by expected value instead lets a narrow,
high-margin category beat a wide, high-probability one on a technicality —
its `p_sku` denominator is smaller — and offers candy to a customer we are
90.6% sure wants a beverage.
:::

::: {#d-bestseller .node-detail}
### Best-Seller {.orange-head}

**The popularity ranking — and the path for about 68% of fills.**

You enter the ALS factor matrix only by having bought in that category before
the cutoff. Most fuel customers never did:

| | Covered by ALS |
|---|---|
| Scored fills in the held-out period | **31.6%** |
| …of the fills that converted in the offered category | 54.9% |

Measured, not assumed — `validate.py` fails if the published share drifts
more than three points from what the scored table actually contains.

```python
raw = popularity[daypart_items]        # no factors for this shopper
```

This is not a degraded path, it is **the primary one**. Build it first: the
personalised tier is an improvement on top of a fallback you need anyway, and
the vendor-funded revenue does not depend on ALS — it depends on going to SKU
granularity at all.
:::

::: {#d-stage1 .node-detail}
### Stage one · the category {.orange-head}

**Relevance decides this, on probability alone.** Six calibrated models give
six unconditional probabilities; we take the highest one we are *allowed* to
show.

```python
allowed = [c for c in categories
           if c not in NOT_OFFERABLE          # tobacco: a business rule
           and in_stock_and_offerable(c)]     # something to actually sell
category = max(allowed, key=lambda c: p_category[c])
```

**Margin does not get a vote here.** Let expected value pick the category and
a narrow, high-margin category beats a wide, high-probability one on nothing
but a shorter SKU tail — `p_sku` is normalised *within* a category, so a
four-SKU category concentrates its probability where a three-hundred-SKU one
spreads it thin. That is how a customer we are 90% sure wants a beverage ends
up being offered candy.

**Ties go to the daypart's best seller**, not to the alphabet. Before that
rule a shopper with every category at the probability floor — someone who has
fuelled a thousand times and never walked in — was shown **beer**, because
"Beer" sorts first.
:::

::: {#d-stage2 .node-detail}
### Stage two · the SKU {.orange-head}

Rank the SKUs **inside that one category**. A SKU from any other category
cannot appear, however profitable.

```python
p_sku  = raw / raw.sum()          # normalised within the category
p_buys = p_category * p_sku       # P(buys this exact SKU on this fill)
order  = argsort(-p_buys)[:10]
```

**Ranked on probability, not on expected value.** The catalog's margins are
average price × an assumed 40% — the PDI extract has no cost column — so
ranking on EV would let an assumption choose the item. The margin terms ride
along for the funding conversation; they do not set the order.

`in_stock` and `offerable` filter the *candidates*; they do not change the
denominator. `P(sku | category)` is a conditional over every SKU in the
category, and excluding tobacco by business rule should not inflate what is
left.

[The same function serves the live fill and the batch table — `scoring.py`.
Two copies of this ranking drifted twice, and both times the written table
disagreed with the live answer.]{.muted}
:::

::: {#d-pairs .node-detail}
### Pair affinity {.teal-head}

A different table answering a different question: not *what will they buy*,
but *what SECOND thing could a discount add to the basket*.

| | What it is | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| `cohort_index` | B's rate among A-regulars ÷ the rate among **equally frequent** others | **Gating** |
| `excess` | the same comparison as a difference, in attach points | **Ranking** |
| `headroom` | `1 −` this shopper's own rate of B | don't discount what they already buy |

**Controlling exposure is the whole trick.** Every cohort is defined as "at
least five purchase baskets", so every cohort is a cohort of *heavy shoppers*
and indexes high on nearly everything. The first cut had drink regulars
over-indexing on frozen food at **6.1×** — pure visit frequency. Comparing
against shoppers who buy just as often and do *not* buy the anchor divides
that out.

**Gate on the index, rank on the excess.** Volume alone picks the popular
item: Candy is 18.2% of every second item in a drink basket and looks
obvious, but its index is **1.07** — not a complement, just everywhere. The
index alone picks the tiny one.
:::

::: {#d-second .node-detail}
### The second item {.green-head}

The anchor is what they buy **anyway**, which makes it the one promotion
certain to cost margin and change nothing. This is the offer worth funding.

| Second category | Their rate | Equally frequent others | Index | Excess |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Alternative Snacks** | 6.0% | 3.5% | **1.74** | 2.6 pts |
| Packaged Sweet Snacks | 6.7% | 4.7% | 1.41 | 2.0 pts |
| **Salty Snacks** | 12.2% | 9.4% | 1.30 | **2.8 pts** |
| Candy | 12.2% | 11.4% | 1.07 | 0.8 pts |

**Alcohol is excluded on both sides** as a policy, not a threshold: a beer
anchor returns *no* second item, and alcohol is never offered as one. Beer's
only complement above 1.0 is Liquor at 1.08. Beer remains a legitimate
*anchor* offer.

It ships as `second_category` and `second_category_skus` in the scored table,
populated on **560,690 of 583,583** rows — empty where nothing clears the
gate, which is a real answer rather than a miss.
:::

::: {#d-valid .node-detail}
### Validation {.green-head}

Two models, two different questions, two different checks.

**Stage one is judged on calibration**, because its output is multiplied by
dollars. A model that ranks well but is scaled wrong prices every offer
wrong, and AUC would never show it. All 583,583 held-out fills, by decile of
predicted `P(beverage)`:

| Decile | Predicted | Actual | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0001 | 0.0005 | +0.0004 |
| 5 | 0.0385 | 0.0395 | +0.0009 |
| 9 | 0.1400 | 0.1407 | +0.0008 |
| **10** | **0.3430** | **0.3287** | **−0.0144** |

Calibrated to within a tenth of a point through the middle; **mildly
over-confident in the top decile**, which is exactly where we spend.

**Stage two is judged on whether it named the item they bought.**

| k | SKU Affinity | Store best seller | Lift |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9.1% | 3.2% | 2.8× |
| 10 | **34.3%** | 16.9% | **2.0×** |

Both rankings scored **on the same rows** — comparing ALS rows against
fallback rows would compare two different populations. On fallback rows the
two agree 100.000% of the time, which is the control that says the harness
works.

[`validate.py` — 116 checks. `validate_sku.py` prints the hit@k table.]{.muted}
:::


::: {#d-ev .node-detail}
### Expected value {.green-head}

The naive form is wrong:

```
P(buys) × margin − cost        ← never negative while margin > discount
```

It never asks what would have happened with **no offer**. The real comparison is
between two worlds:

```
show iff   p₁ × (margin − discount)  >  p₀ × margin
```

Worked, per 1,000 fuel visits at 2am. A beverage averages **$3.25**; assume 40%
margin and a **$0.90** discount, the going rate in your own data:

| | No offer | Offer shown |
|---|---|---|
| Buy | 75 | 90 *(assume +1.5 pts)* |
| Margin each | $1.30 | $0.40 |
| **Total** | **$97.50** | **$36.00** |

**−$61.50.** And it gets *worse* at 6am (−$129.90), because the discount reaches
more people who were already buying.

To break even you'd need to more than **triple** the purchase rate. A
self-funded discount of this size cannot pay for itself out of that basket — at
any hour. Which is precisely why every promotion in the data is a vendor
program.

*Margin and lift are assumptions; the data has no cost column. The $3.25 and
$0.90 are real.*
:::

::: {#d-screen .node-detail}
### The pump screen

One offer, or none. The constraints the product has to live inside:

- **Fire during the fill.** 77% of in-store purchases happen within five minutes
  of the fuel transaction.
- **16.2% already shopped** before fuelling. They are not addressable by a pump
  screen, so your real audience is the other 84%.
- Ninety seconds, one screen, and a customer watching the gallons tick.

Showing nothing is a legitimate output. It needs no model to execute and it
never loses money — which makes it the baseline every offer must beat.
:::

::: {#d-holdout .node-detail}
### Holdout {.red-head}

**This does not exist, and it is the single thing worth asking Murphy for.**

A slice of pumps that show no offer, assigned at random. Without it you can
measure what people *do*, never what an offer *changed*.

```python
# Random at the visit level, logged with the decision.
holdout = F.hash("fuel_tx") % 100 < 5     # 5% see nothing
```

Log the offer you showed **and the probability you showed it with**. Without
logged propensities you cannot evaluate offline later, and that mistake is
unrecoverable — the information was never captured.

With a holdout you can finally model **uplift** rather than propensity, and
separate the persuadable customers from the ones who would have bought anyway.
:::

::: {#d-did .node-detail}
### Staggered adoption {.red-head}

The second-best design, available today — and the one whose assumptions our data
violates.

Your `discounts` table records **redemptions, not impressions**: 9,215,074
transactions with a discount applied, and **zero** records of an offer shown and
declined. `P(buy | offered)` has no denominator.

But stores switch promotions on at different dates:

| Promotion | Stores | First | Median | Last |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `loyaltyDiscount` | 188 | 10/2024 | **01/2026** | 09/2026 |
| `Skupos` | 167 | 10/2024 | 11/2024 | 07/2026 |

Monster's share of beverage lines around each store's promo start:

| Weeks | Stores | Share |
|---|---|---|
| −12 | 24 | 8.82% |
| −1 | 49 | 10.95% |
| **0** | **280** | 11.55% |
| +12 | 273 | 11.79% |

**Don't believe the +1.7 points.** The store count jumps 49 → 280 at week 0, so
almost nobody has a pre-period, and the apparent pre-trend is the sample growing
from 24 to 49 stores rather than behaviour changing.

The design is sound; this estimate is not. A balanced panel of late adopters
would fix it — and it is a better argument for the holdout than any amount of
methodology.
:::

:::

:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  const svg = document.getElementById("pipeline-svg");
  if (!svg) return;
  const panes = document.querySelectorAll(".node-detail");
  const show = (id) => {
    let found = false;
    panes.forEach((p) => {
      const on = p.id === id;
      p.classList.toggle("is-active", on);
      if (on) found = true;
    });
    if (!found) show("d-start");
  };
  show("d-start");

  svg.querySelectorAll("g.node").forEach((g) => {
    const t = g.querySelector("title");
    if (!t) return;
    const name = t.textContent.trim();
    if (!document.getElementById("d-" + name)) return;
    g.classList.add("is-clickable");
    const pick = () => {
      svg.querySelectorAll("g.node").forEach((o) =>
        o.classList.remove("is-selected"));
      g.classList.add("is-selected");
      show("d-" + name);
    };
    g.addEventListener("click", pick);
    g.setAttribute("tabindex", "0");
    g.setAttribute("role", "button");
    g.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
      if (e.key === "Enter" || e.key === " ") { e.preventDefault(); pick(); }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
```
